newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: US, Russia negotiators seek anti-missile compromise.
newsitem.headline: US, Russia negotiators seek anti-missile compromise.

text.p: U.S. and Russian disarmament envoys resumed negotiations on Friday seeking to salvage an accord on regional missile defences, officials said.
A signing ceremony planned for Geneva on Thursday was called off at the last moment -- leading the two powers to blame each other for the hold-up after years of negotiations.
Moscow's delegation still hopes for a compromise and expects closed-door talks in Geneva over the weekend, according to a Russian diplomat.
"They are still continuing negotiations. It is difficult to say what the outcome will be," he told Reuters.
"Our delegation is hoping that a compromise can be reached. We are optimistic it can be worked out," he added.
A spokesman at the U.S. diplomatic mission, declining to give details of any meeting, said: "Negotiations are continuing. There have been contacts among the delegations today."
He could not say whether there was any chance of the deal being done and documents being signed. "If there is a prospect of a signature, we will let you know."
The five delegations held meetings overnight, according to officials.

Belarus, Kazakhstan, Russia, Ukraine and the United States are the five countries taking part in the treaty's so-called Standing Consultative Commission which oversees implementation of the ABM (anti-ballistic missile) pact, signed in 1972 by the United States and Russia.

The pact is widely considered a cornerstone of international arms control, but the issue of which systems it should allow has bedevilled U.S.-Russian arms talks since the "Star Wars" days of the 1980s.
The ABM treaty limits defences against strategic -- or long-range -- missiles but was not meant to address regional -- or so-called "theatre" -- missile defences.
Moscow has been suspicious that the United States was trying to develop an anti-missile shield that would render the whole Russian strategic arsenal useless.

U.S. President Bill Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin last year asked negotiators to define which systems were strategic -- and hence limited by the ABM treaty -- and which were smaller-scale "theatre" systems which are not limited.
Experts from the five states worked out phase one draft accords in June on lower-speed anti-missile systems, leaving faster systems to be negotiated later in a part two agreement.

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher and Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov announced last month they had approved the first phase which would specify which short-range defence missile systems are allowed under the ABM treaty.

At their September meeting in New York, they agreed to permit deployment of lower-speed theatre missile defence systems of up to three km (two miles) per second provided they are not tested against faster, longer-range ballistic missile targets.
The U.S.-Russian statement committed both sides to conclude part one and to sign documents, and to continue negotiating a second phase, according to U.S. officials in Washington.

"What the Russians have effectively done here is try to merge elements of part one and part two, which, of course, is contrary to the joint statement that was issued in late September," Statement Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said in Washington on Thursday.
"What we would like to do is convince them that we need to go back to the September agreement, sign those documents, keep on negotiating on part two, keep this process going," he added.

On Wednesday, the U.S. State Department announced that the signing ceremony had been called off and accused Russia of reversing its position. The next day, Russia suggested it was Washington which had blocked signature.

Stanley Riveles, head of the U.S. delegation to the Standing Consultative Commission, is leading Washington's team to the talks. Russian Deputy Minister Georgy Mamedov is in Geneva heading his country's delegation.
